headline: Budget changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing are positive for housing equity and budget repair, while falling prices improve first-home buyer affordability
reasoning: Koukoulas sees the CGT and negative gearing changes as meaningful equity and tax-system reforms, with revenue benefits that grow materially in years 4-7 of the budget, helping move the fiscal position toward neutral. First-home buyers are well-positioned: small-deposit schemes guaranteed by the Commonwealth, falling prices, rates likely on hold, and modest wage growth all improve affordability. He expects this cohort to provide market support.
quote: For the first time buyers, of course, they're sitting really pretty right now because not only can they get access to a property with a relatively small deposit, with the the difference of the loan guaranteed by the Commonwealth government, but with prices falling, uh, interest rates probably on hold, and even with modest wage increases, all of a sudden the affordability equation for many first time buyers is there. So I think that's going to be where the support is going to be in the housing market, partly because of the tax changes, partly because of the macro environment.
episode_title: Does Australia really have a productivity problem?

headline: Koukoulas sees RBA rate-hike cycle effectively done, with 5%-plus cash rate scenario off the table
reasoning: Koukoulas argues the three rate hikes in the first half of the year are working, as business confidence and consumer sentiment are weakening markedly and price indicators such as expected selling prices, expected wage increases, and input costs are all tilting lower after the spike caused by Middle East conflict and oil reaching $100/barrel. He notes the possibility of one more hike but says it would require quite remarkable news — a lower unemployment rate and an upside inflation surprise — which he views as unlikely given the slowing economy.
quote: The three rate hikes in the first half of this year are working. Uh, we're seeing some, uh, concerns in both, uh, business confidence, consumer sentiment, these sorts of measures... some of the more worrying concerns that we'd have to have, you know, a series of more rate hikes, a cash rate of 5% plus, which was doing the rounds fairly recently, are no longer valid. That it's just this question about maybe, just maybe there's one more rate hike, but it would require yeah, quite remarkable news on growth.
episode_title: Does Australia really have a productivity problem?

headline: Australia may simply lag the US by a few years in capturing AI-driven productivity gains, rather than having a structural productivity problem
reasoning: Koukoulas notes that non-mining business investment is rising and much of it is going into data centres, which is positive. He suggests Australia could be 2-3 years behind the US in realising AI productivity benefits as the technology is applied to more industries. More broadly, he questions whether Australia truly has a productivity problem, noting that productivity is nearly impossible to measure in a services-dominated economy where over three-quarters of jobs and output are in services. He references the well-known observation that productivity gains are 'showing up everywhere except in the data.'
quote: It may maybe we're just lagging a couple of years and so that in a few years time, we'll get the benefits of AI doing a lot of the menial and other tasks that it's currently being applied to in certain, uh, industries in the US. So that's part of the issue. The other part of the productivity issue is that I'm, I'm not convinced that we've got a productivity problem... when you when you're moving to a services economy like we've got in Australia now, where over three quarters of our, uh, jobs and output are in the services sector, productivity is really, really hard to measure and in fact impossible to measure in some instances. So I'm wondering whether we're sort of having a, a real conniption over something that isn't really that much of a problem.
episode_title: Does Australia really have a productivity problem?

headline: Koukoulas sees Australian economy heading into sub-trend growth with falling inflation and rising unemployment through late 2026
reasoning: Koukoulas characterises the current Australian economic trajectory as broadly moving in the RBA's desired direction: growth is solid but slowing, wages growth is contained within the inflation target, global conditions are not adding upside inflation pressure, and unemployment is low but rising in trend terms. He expects sub-trend growth, a higher unemployment rate, and falling inflation in the second half of 2026. He believes the earlier fear of a 5%-plus cash rate is no longer valid, and that another rate hike would require a remarkable upside surprise in growth, employment, and inflation data.
quote: Growth is solid, but it's slowing. Wages growth is sort of okay, but it's well in contention with the inflation target. Global conditions seem to be not imposing that upside to inflation pressures. And the unemployment rate is still relatively low, but it's increasing in trend terms. So you put all them into the melting pot. You've got this position where we're heading for the second half of 2026 with sub trend economic growth almost certainly a higher unemployment rate, inflation will fall.
episode_title: Does Australia really have a productivity problem?

headline: Koukoulas warns falling house prices and rising building costs risk derailing the construction pipeline and dragging on GDP into 2027
reasoning: Koukoulas explains that if future house prices are expected to fall 10% while building costs rise at 4-5%, it becomes uneconomic for builders to complete projects. He flags that the recent uptrend in building approvals may not translate into completions, which are what the economy actually needs. This dynamic creates a negative wealth effect on consumer spending and risks a negative surprise for GDP in late 2026 and into 2027 as supply chains and labour serving the building sector are affected.
quote: If we get this dynamic where future house prices are expected to be falling, say 10%, and your building costs are increasing even at a modest rate, say 5% 4% with your materials and labor costs and these sorts of things pretty quickly. It doesn't pay the builders to build that property. So even though we've got that nice uptrend in building approvals over the last 12 months, they're just approvals. They're not completions. And we need more completions. So in a funny way it is actually negative for GDP growth. Because if you're supplying those building companies with the materials and the labor, you could be in for a bit of a negative surprise in the latter part of this year, and certainly to 2027, if this house price momentum continues to be sort of accelerating to the downside.
episode_title: Does Australia really have a productivity problem?
